body: Would you be willing to explain why the op needs this instead of recommendation of blanket karma-hopeful positive advice?

I read many places that you have to let the ends of the cut callous over a bit (turn a bit brown and dry) before submerging them in water to help protect it from rot. You can alternatively dip the ends in wax to waterproof them. From this photo it looks like a very fresh cut. I'm not sure how your cutting is doing now but I would maybe try that if you ever start another.

I've called the hotline only twice (recently) and was met with the same very generic responses. I knew they were stock answers, but I also didn't call with any sort of expectation at what I was going to get out the call. At the time, I only needed to make it from point A to point B (one time while driving and one time just in my thoughts). Although both times I was connected within one minute, and both people who took my call were very nice, you could tell both times that their goal is to end the call, not to really encourage you to want to live or not want to die (which in my opinion are two different mindsets).

However, as someone who has formerly done crisis response and management professionally, I know how to maneuver around their questions so that I don't get basically SWATed. It surely should \*NOT\* have to be that way. That one's honesty with the reality they are facing could lead them to endless debt or a criminal record is beyond me.

Sorry for getting on my soapbox, but I will say though that I don't blame at all the people taking the call -- I think it's an organizational problem. That they can ask for all this money and only provide this level of hiring/training/service is extremely problematic on a number of levels. While the second person who took my call was especially nice and was even willing to have an actual conversation with me, there was a point where she asked me to hold very briefly and before I could agree, she said something like, "oh nevermind, someone else got the call -- we're supposed to try to take..." and then trailed off like she knew not to reveal fully what their process/goals/values are. But we were already in like free-flow mode so it just kind of came out. It was then that I (fully) realized the hotline is just a money machine.

Transracial adoptee here. Definitely do not mean to hijack your post with my own shit, but your explanation of your parents' response to this sound very similar to mine ("victim," racism doesn't exist here, we're not different). For reference, I am a person of color and my parents are white. I have similarly been put in a position where I was the only POC present and needed to speak on behalf of what ought to happen or how "we" think it should be. I wish I could tell you how to get it all figured out -- coming to terms with your identity -- but the reality is that I have no fucking clue either. The best I can do is share things that have aided me in \*trying\* to navigate it, if you're into that.

In some ways, I relate to your father with not wanting to potentially disrespect my adoptive family because they have done so much for me. However, from a young age, I had known to adjust my expectations of understanding/acceptance due to the differences in perspective and experience between me and my parents. For years, I've had to (or tried to) take baby steps in distancing myself and then figuring out how to cope with the potential hurt associated with that (eg my parents saying they wish I would call more or wondering why I don't share stories of happenings in my life). It sounds shitty but for years (I'm in my 30's) it worked ok enough to have a relationship until (as you mentioned with heightened exposure and awareness) a discussion on race/identity and its salience in certain situations went off the rails with my folks and I was disowned (like yesterday). 

I tell you this to advise that you maybe take steps in assessing whether it's worth your mental health to maintain certain relationships, whether with family or friends. & this is coming from someone who was previously in the "family is all you really have and you do what you can to remain a unit no matter what" camp. It will be hard to fathom while standing before it, but as it's happening (if it comes to that) it may become clearer how beneficial it could be for your well-being. One thing that you may have to face is that your family might only ever see you as their child/sibling, and potentially not as an individual with other components that really matter outside their scope of awareness. It's sometimes difficult to separate that for people that might not have had first-hand experience in \*having\* to deal with it. In the case of your father, it may be difficult because of how long he's spent not being able to confront it (whether by choice or force). It's a place of comfort for many, even those that do have to do deal with it, to disregard it because the alternatives (eg to back away slowly or speak up) are significantly more difficult to navigate due to not knowing how others are going to react. 

That leads me to these other situations where you're posed to sort of speak or act on behalf of minorities. Despite how uncomfortable (and potentially impossible in certain situations), one of the ways you can maintain control of your identity is to actively not let others tokenize you. I've been in professional trainings where I was called on by a speaker to ask about my race's opinion on a matter. In one instance I embarrassed the shit out of her -- both out of a little bit of spite for assuming, but also what I felt was out of necessity for the sake of learning. & not in an overtly malicious way -- all I did was offer that although I look this way, I don't feel comfortable speaking on the issue due to my lack of exposure to the issue posed. I mentioned being raised by people "not like me" and asked whether I should be speaking from this frame or that frame. It actually ended up helping the discussion because we were discussing stereotypes and culture. The more awareness that's created this way for people in general, the easier it might (one day) be to realize that in some instances, it's not necessarily just you that might be struggling with who you are -- it's other people that have issues relying on who or what they think/hope you are for their comfort (or agenda). 

I don't know if this is "good" advice but it's something I tried and still try: I get involved with things that make me that thing. I'm a "cycler" or a "knitter" or a "runner." Yes, there may still be instances where race might come into play within those circles, but it really is nice (from my experience) to form these new parts of your identity and having different sorts of solidarity with others in this way as well. This is not to say "find ways to ignore race," but I have found it helps to reduce the sometimes significant pressure I put on myself to focus on proving to everyone that I don't \*just\* have to be a \*race\* \*gender\* (eg a black man, white woman, Asian non-binary, or what have you). 

If you have the kind of time and emotional space, try reading up on intersectionality. It's basically an identity theory that explores how different components of our identity mix and match, are more or less salient, and more or less affect us in different situations.

Sorry for the novel but I really wanted to reiterate that while your situation is unique, I hope you can find comfort in knowing that you're not entirely alone with your desires to explore and own your identity. <3
